source_note: Group values follow IARC Monograph hazard classifications (monographs.iarc.who.int/list-of-classifications), cross-checked against FDA/EU regulatory actions and California Prop 65 where noted. 'NE' means IARC has not evaluated the substance — IARC states explicitly that for unclassified agents, no determination of non-carcinogenicity or overall safety should be inferred, so NE means 'unknown', never 'safe'. 'CLEAR' marks substances specifically studied and cleared by regulators, included so the app is not only ever flagging things. IARC groups describe STRENGTH OF EVIDENCE that an agent can cause cancer under some exposure condition — not the risk at the dose present in a given product.

groups.3: Evaluated by IARC — evidence insufficient to classify
groups.CLEAR: Specifically studied and cleared by regulators

entries.name: Red 3 (Erythrosine)
entries.found_in: Candy, baked goods, frostings, maraschino cherries
entries.note: Not IARC-classified. FDA banned it from US food and ingested drugs in Jan 2025 under the Delaney Clause after it caused thyroid tumours in male rats; food phase-out runs through Jan 2027. Banned in cosmetics since 1990.

entries.name: Titanium dioxide
entries.found_in: Chewing gum, icing, sauces; sunscreen, toothpaste, cosmetics
entries.note: IARC 2B based on INHALATION studies (occupational dust), not ingestion. Banned as a food additive in the EU since 2022; still permitted in the US.

entries.name: Caramel colour (Class III/IV)
entries.found_in: Colas, dark sauces, gravies, beer
entries.note: Not IARC-classified as a whole. Ammonia-process versions (Class III/IV) contain 4-MEI, which is California Prop 65 listed on animal evidence.

entries.name: Red 40 (Allura Red)
entries.found_in: Soft drinks, cereals, candy, snacks
entries.note: IARC evaluated; evidence insufficient to classify. Separately monitored for behavioural effects in children — a different concern from cancer.

entries.name: Yellow 5 (Tartrazine)
entries.found_in: Soft drinks, chips, cereals, pickles
entries.note: Not IARC-classified as a carcinogen. A known allergen and behavioural trigger for some children; tracked separately from cancer risk.

entries.name: Yellow 6 (Sunset Yellow)
entries.found_in: Cheese snacks, candy, baked goods
entries.note: Not IARC-classified as a carcinogen. Historically watched for benzidine contamination from older manufacturing processes.

entries.name: Blue 1 (Brilliant Blue)
entries.found_in: Candy, drinks, ice cream
entries.note: Not IARC-classified.

entries.name: Blue 2 (Indigotine)
entries.found_in: Candy, pet food, baked goods
entries.note: Not IARC-classified. Some very-high-dose rodent studies are cited by advocacy groups but have not been confirmed by regulators.

entries.name: Green 3 (Fast Green)
entries.found_in: Canned peas, candy, mint-flavoured products
entries.note: Not IARC-classified. Banned as a food colour in the EU; permitted in the US.

entries.name: Citrus Red 2
entries.found_in: Applied to the skin of some Florida oranges
entries.note: IARC 2B. Permitted only on orange peel in the US, not in the flesh, and not in juice.

entries.name: Nitrite / nitrate curing salts
entries.found_in: Bacon, ham, hot dogs, deli meat, cured fish
entries.note: IARC 2A for ingested nitrite/nitrate under conditions leading to nitrosamine formation in the body. Vitamin C in the product reduces that conversion.

entries.name: Nitrosamines (NDMA)
entries.found_in: Formed in cured meats, beer, some cheeses; not an added ingredient
entries.note: A reaction product rather than an ingredient. Forms when nitrites meet amines under heat or stomach acid.

entries.name: Potassium bromate
entries.found_in: Some breads, rolls, pizza dough (US)
entries.note: Banned as a food additive in the EU, UK, Canada, Brazil and China. Still permitted in limited US uses. California requires a warning label.

entries.name: BHA
entries.found_in: Cereals, chips, chewing gum, oils, food packaging
entries.note: California Prop 65 listed. Used as an antioxidant to stop fats going rancid.

entries.name: BHT
entries.found_in: Cereals, snack foods, chewing gum, cosmetics
entries.note: IARC evaluated; evidence insufficient to classify. Restricted in some countries but widely permitted.

entries.name: Benzoates
entries.found_in: Soft drinks, fruit juices, pickles, salad dressings
entries.note: Not carcinogen-classified. Separate concern: can form trace benzene (a Group 1 carcinogen) when combined with vitamin C plus heat or light.

entries.name: Benzene
entries.found_in: Not an added ingredient — a trace contaminant in some drinks and personal-care products
entries.note: IARC Group 1, and named by WHO as a chemical of major public health concern. In food it appears as a contaminant, notably from benzoate plus ascorbic acid reactions.

entries.name: Propyl gallate
entries.found_in: Oils, shortening, meat products, chewing gum
entries.note: Not formally IARC-classified; long-term human data is limited.

entries.name: TBHQ
entries.found_in: Fried foods, crackers, instant noodles, frozen foods
entries.note: Not IARC-classified. Permitted at low limits; some advocacy groups petition for review, and regulators maintain current approvals.

entries.name: Aspartame
entries.found_in: Diet soft drinks, tabletop sweeteners, chewing gum, some medicines
entries.note: Classified 2B in 2023 (IARC Volume 134) on limited evidence in humans, limited in animals, limited mechanistic. WHO/JECFA reviewed the same evidence and left the acceptable daily intake unchanged.

entries.name: Saccharin
entries.found_in: Tabletop sweeteners, diet drinks, some toothpaste
entries.note: Downgraded from 2B after the rat bladder-tumour mechanism was shown not to apply to humans. A good example of a classification being revised as science improved.

entries.name: Sucralose
entries.found_in: Diet drinks, protein powders, baked goods, sauces
entries.note: Not IARC-classified. A 2023 study raised genotoxicity questions about a breakdown product; FDA and EFSA maintain current approvals pending further review.

entries.name: Acesulfame potassium
entries.found_in: Diet drinks, yoghurt, chewing gum, often blended with other sweeteners
entries.note: Not IARC-classified; long-term human data is limited.

entries.name: Cyclamate
entries.found_in: Sweeteners outside the US; banned in US food since 1970
entries.note: IARC Group 3 — the 1970s rat bladder-tumour findings were not reproduced and are not considered relevant to humans, but the US ban remains in place.

entries.name: Acrylamide
entries.found_in: Formed by high-heat cooking: chips, fries, toast, coffee, crackers
entries.note: A processing by-product, never an added ingredient. Forms when starchy foods are fried, baked or roasted above about 120C. Darker browning means more acrylamide.

entries.name: Benzo[a]pyrene / PAHs
entries.found_in: Grilled, charred and smoked foods; liquid smoke flavouring
entries.note: Benzo[a]pyrene itself is IARC Group 1. Forms when fat drips onto flames or when food is smoked. Reduced by lower-temperature cooking and trimming fat.

entries.name: Processed meat
entries.found_in: Bacon, ham, sausages, hot dogs, deli slices, jerky
entries.note: IARC Group 1 — sufficient evidence in humans for colorectal cancer. Applies to meat transformed by salting, curing, fermenting or smoking. Group 1 reflects certainty of the hazard, not the size of the risk.

entries.name: Red meat
entries.found_in: Unprocessed beef, pork, lamb, veal
entries.note: IARC 2A on limited human evidence plus strong mechanistic and animal data. Distinct from the Group 1 processed-meat finding.

entries.name: Alcohol (ethanol)
entries.found_in: Alcoholic drinks; also a solvent in some flavourings and extracts
entries.note: IARC Group 1 across multiple cancer sites — breast, liver, colorectal, oesophageal, oral. No threshold below which risk is known to be absent.

entries.name: Acetaldehyde
entries.found_in: Alcohol metabolism; trace amounts in some flavourings and ripe fruit
entries.note: IARC Group 1 in the context of alcohol metabolism. Occurs naturally in trace amounts in many foods.

entries.name: Aflatoxins
entries.found_in: Improperly stored corn, peanuts, tree nuts, dried fruit, spices
entries.note: A mould toxin, not an ingredient. IARC Group 1, strongly linked to liver cancer. Tightly regulated, but trace contamination can occur.

entries.name: Ochratoxin A
entries.found_in: Cereals, coffee, dried fruit, wine, spices
entries.note: Another storage mould toxin. Regulated to low limits in most countries.

entries.name: Asian-style pickled vegetables
entries.found_in: Traditional salt-pickled vegetables, chiefly in East Asian diets
entries.note: IARC 2B for the traditional preparation method, which can produce N-nitroso compounds. Modern commercial pickling differs substantially.

entries.name: Coffee
entries.found_in: Coffee and coffee-flavoured products
entries.note: Moved from Group 2B to Group 3 in 2016 — IARC found the evidence insufficient to classify it as carcinogenic. Included because the old 2B listing is still widely misquoted.

entries.name: Methyleugenol
entries.found_in: Natural essential oils — basil, allspice, nutmeg; some flavourings and fragrances
entries.note: Upgraded from 2B to Group 2A in 2023 (IARC Volume 134) on sufficient animal evidence plus strong mechanistic evidence. Occurs naturally rather than being added synthetically in most cases.

entries.name: Isoeugenol
entries.found_in: Fragrances and flavourings; naturally in ylang-ylang and nutmeg oils
entries.note: Classified 2B in 2023 (IARC Volume 134) on sufficient evidence in experimental animals; human evidence inadequate.

entries.name: Safrole
entries.found_in: Sassafras oil and some spices; banned as a US food additive
entries.note: IARC 2B. Banned from US food since 1960 after rodent liver-tumour findings.

entries.name: Coumarin
entries.found_in: Cassia cinnamon, tonka bean, some flavourings
entries.note: IARC Group 3 for cancer. The regulatory concern is liver toxicity at high intake, not carcinogenicity — which is why cassia cinnamon carries intake guidance in the EU.

entries.name: PFOA
entries.found_in: Grease-resistant wrappers, microwave popcorn bags, non-stick coatings
entries.note: Reclassified to Group 1 in 2023. Not a food ingredient — a contaminant that migrates from packaging and cookware.

entries.name: PFOS
entries.found_in: Same packaging and coating sources as PFOA
entries.note: Classified Group 2B in 2023. Like PFOA, a contaminant rather than an intentional ingredient.

entries.name: Phthalates (DEHP)
entries.found_in: Flexible plastics, tubing, some fragrances and nail products
entries.note: Not a food ingredient — a plasticiser that can migrate into fatty foods. Also used as a fragrance carrier in cosmetics.

entries.name: BPA
entries.found_in: Can linings, hard polycarbonate plastics, thermal receipt paper
entries.note: Not IARC-classified as a carcinogen. The principal regulatory concern is endocrine disruption — a separate question from cancer.

entries.name: 1,4-Dioxane
entries.found_in: Trace by-product in ethoxylated surfactants — shampoo, body wash, detergent
entries.note: Never listed as an ingredient because it is an unintended by-product of the ethoxylation process. Reduced by vacuum stripping during manufacture.

entries.name: Styrene
entries.found_in: Polystyrene foam containers and cups
entries.note: Classified 2A. Migration into food is greatest with hot, fatty or acidic contents.

entries.name: Formaldehyde and formaldehyde-releasers
entries.found_in: Shampoos, hair straighteners, nail products, some cosmetics
entries.note: Formaldehyde itself is IARC Group 1. Rarely listed by that name — usually present via preservatives that slowly release it, which is why the releaser names are matched here.

entries.name: Talc
entries.found_in: Body powder, face powder, blush, some tablets
entries.note: IARC 2B. Risk has historically been tied to talc contaminated with asbestiform fibres; cosmetic-grade talc is regulated to exclude these.

entries.name: Coal tar
entries.found_in: Anti-dandruff and psoriasis shampoos, some hair dyes
entries.note: IARC Group 1. Still used medicinally because it is effective against scaling; exposure is intended to be limited and short-term.

entries.name: Parabens
entries.found_in: Preservatives in lotions, shampoos, makeup, some foods
entries.note: Not IARC-classified as carcinogenic. The ongoing scientific debate concerns endocrine activity — a separate question from cancer.

entries.name: p-Phenylenediamine
entries.found_in: Permanent hair dyes, some temporary tattoos
entries.note: IARC Group 3 for cancer. A significant contact allergen, which is the main documented risk.

entries.name: Ethylene oxide and ethoxylated ingredients
entries.found_in: Sterilising agent; not listed as a cosmetic or food ingredient
entries.note: IARC Group 1. Not an ingredient you will see on a label — it is used to sterilise equipment and spices, and is the process chemical behind ethoxylated ingredients (PEGs, -eth compounds). Those ingredients are not themselves Group 1; their associated concern is trace 1,4-dioxane, listed separately.

entries.name: Methylene chloride
entries.found_in: Historically a decaffeination solvent; paint strippers, degreasers
entries.note: Classified 2A on limited human evidence plus sufficient animal evidence. Most decaf coffee now uses water or CO2 processes instead.

entries.name: Ethylene dichloride
entries.found_in: Industrial solvent; historic extraction uses
entries.note: Group 2B on sufficient animal evidence. JECFA considers it unsuitable for use in food processing.

entries.name: MSG (Monosodium glutamate)
entries.found_in: Savoury snacks, soups, sauces, seasoning blends
entries.note: No credible evidence of carcinogenicity. Among the most extensively studied additives; FDA and EFSA classify it as safe at normal use levels.

entries.name: Carrageenan
entries.found_in: Dairy alternatives, ice cream, deli meats, toothpaste
entries.note: Food-grade carrageenan is not carcinogen-classified. Degraded carrageenan ('poligeenan') is a chemically distinct substance not used in food — the two are frequently confused.

entries.name: Xanthan gum
entries.found_in: Sauces, dressings, gluten-free baking, cosmetics
entries.note: A fermentation-derived thickener with no carcinogenicity concerns identified by regulators.

entries.name: Citric acid
entries.found_in: Widespread — drinks, candy, canned goods, cosmetics
entries.note: Occurs naturally in citrus fruit; commercially produced by fermentation. No carcinogenicity concerns.

entries.name: Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C)
entries.found_in: Added to cured meats, drinks and cereals as a preservative and nutrient
entries.note: Not a carcinogen. In cured meats it actively REDUCES nitrosamine formation, which is why it often appears alongside nitrite curing salts.

entries.name: Lecithin
entries.found_in: Chocolate, baked goods, margarine, infant formula
entries.note: An emulsifier derived from soy, sunflower or egg. No carcinogenicity concerns identified.
